source_text: Ad exemplandam et confirmandam iudicii sui aequitatem iuramento Deus utitur et auctoritatem constituti obtestatione cumulat. Intellexit hoc genus loquendi Apostolus, qui ad Hebraeos ita disseruit: Volens, inquit, Deus ostendere, promissionis haeredibus immobilitatem consilii sui interposuit iusiurandum, ut per duas res immobiles, quibus impossibile est mentiri Deum, fortissimum solacium habeamus [n52] .
pass_a_gloss: To exemplify and confirm the fairness of his judgment God uses an oath and heaps the authority of the decree by obtestation. The Apostle understood this kind of speaking, who to the Hebrews discoursed thus: God, he says, wishing to show to the heirs of the promise the immobility of his counsel interposed an oath, that through two immobile things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we may have the strongest solace.
pass_b_english: To illustrate and confirm the fairness of his judgment, God uses an oath, adding a solemn pledge to the authority of his decree. The apostle understood this manner of speaking when he explained to the Hebrews: ‘God, wishing to show the heirs of the promise the unchangeable nature of his purpose, intervened with an oath, so that through two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we might have the strongest encouragement’ (Hebrews 6:17–18).

choices.why: Paul in Julian's citations; keep Apostle not 'Paul' unless Paulus is written.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
